lesson.title: Valleys in the Neighborhood: What Makes a Local Minimum
lesson.summary: A local minimum is a point where a function dips to a value at least as small as everything nearby, the valley counterpart to a local maximum, and it need not be the lowest value the function ever takes.
lesson.body:
A function has a local minimum at x = c if there is some open interval around c, contained in the domain of f, on which f(c) is less than or equal to f(x) for every x in that interval. Structurally this is the mirror image of the local maximum definition from the previous section, with the inequality flipped. As with local maxima, a differentiable function that has a local minimum at c must have a horizontal tangent there, f'(c) = 0, because the function has to stop falling and start rising right at the bottom of the valley.

Continue with the same running example, f(x) = x^3 - 3x over all real numbers, and look now at the second place its derivative f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 vanishes, at x = 1. First, f(1) = 1^3 - 3(1) = 1 - 3 = -2. Test a point slightly to the right, x = 1.1: f(1.1) = (1.1)^3 - 3(1.1) = 1.331 - 3.3 = -1.969, which is greater than -2. Test a point slightly to the left, x = 0.9: f(0.9) = (0.9)^3 - 3(0.9) = 0.729 - 2.7 = -1.971, also greater than -2. Both nearby values exceed f(1) = -2, matching the local minimum definition exactly, so f has a local minimum at x = 1, with local minimum value -2. And as expected, f'(1) = 3(1)^2 - 3 = 3 - 3 = 0, so the tangent line is indeed horizontal there.

This minimum, too, is only local. Follow f(x) = x^3 - 3x out to very large negative x, and the x^3 term again dominates, this time sending f(x) toward negative infinity, so the function keeps producing outputs smaller than -2 far to the left. The valley at x = 1 is real within its own neighborhood but is not the lowest point the function ever reaches overall.

Step back and notice the pattern shared by both of the last two sections: at both x = -1 and x = 1, the local extremum coincided exactly with a point where the derivative was zero. That is not a coincidence specific to this cubic, it reflects a general fact about how differentiable functions behave at peaks and valleys, and it is the observation that the next section turns into a formal, named definition: the critical point.
